name: Heartland Beef
blurb: One big packing plant in Prairie Bend, 1,400 line workers, and about 600 ranches that sell it cattle. Founder Walt Dreyer started as a rancher and holds 28% of the vote.

directors.name: Carla Whitfield
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You are outside counsel and have seen the complaint numbers. Heartland is your firm's biggest client, and refunding every fee puts an admission in writing. You prefer fixing the process with confirmation calls and keeping admissions out of the record.

directors.name: Denise Kowalski
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: You speak for plant workers. A rancher boycott or a sales drop means fewer hours on the line, and the fired field staff were your members' cousins. You want the abuse stopped without the profit division collapsing, so you favor stronger checks.

directors.name: Marcus Feld
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 9% and told investors the program count was why you bought. Privately, your lender told you the credit line is priced off that count: below 3.0 the rate steps up a point, about $9 million a year. Ending targets costs real money.

directors.name: Gus Halvorsen
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.home: Walt Dreyer, the founder (hunting partner of 30 years)
directors.motive: Walt Dreyer has been your hunting partner for thirty years and hired Karen Mueller himself. He will not believe the complaints without proof. Voting to end targets or move her out would read as a vote against him, so you want time.

directors.name: Luanne Pruitt
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You lead the ranchers' co-op whose members found fees on their checks. You want the refund and an apology, but Heartland is the only buyer within a day's haul and a boycott would hurt your own herd too.

directors.name: Howard Lindqvist
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.motive: You signed the last three audits and reviewed the program count. Ending the targets says the metric you approved was the problem, and removing Mueller blames one person. A six-month study keeps the questions pointed away from your signature.

briefing.intro: Heartland Beef runs one packing plant with 1,400 line workers and about 600 supplier ranches. Founder Walt Dreyer holds 28% of the vote, and the annual shareholder meeting is in five weeks.
facts: Reps are paid a bonus for each add-on program, such as hauling, feed credit or insurance, that a rancher or grocer joins, under the slogan "five programs per account." The average has risen from 2.1 to 4.6, and analysts and lenders treat it as proof of customer loyalty.

A newspaper plans a story in ten days about reps who enrolled ranchers in fee-charging programs without their knowledge. The ethics hotline logged 650 enrollment complaints in two years, and 230 field staff were fired, mostly at the lowest levels.
Karen Mueller runs the sales division, which brings in 60% of profit. She calls it a handful of cheaters and says the targets are fair, and her own bonus rides on the count.
Dropping the targets could cut the program count by half in two years and the stock ($52) by 15% or more. Keeping them risks fines and lawsuits if the newspaper story lands first.
Improper fees are estimated at $4 million to $40 million. Ranchers are angry, and a boycott by a quarter of them would leave the plant short of cattle.

options.title: End targets and refund
options.text: Drop the bonus, refund every disputed fee and bring in an outside firm; the program count and the stock are expected to fall.

options.title: Keep targets, add checks
options.text: Keep the bonus, add confirmation calls to ranchers and fire anyone caught; ranchers may say it blames the bottom of the ladder.

options.title: Study first
options.text: Change nothing now and hire an outside firm to report in six months; the newspaper story runs in ten days with no answer.

options.title: Replace the sales head
options.text: Move Karen Mueller out of sales and let an interim head decide on targets; the division brings in 60% of profit.

reveal.text: The real firm was Wells Fargo, whose goal was eight products per household. Employees opened accounts customers had not asked for, regulators fined the bank $185 million in 2016, and about 5,300 employees were fired. The directors' later report found the board's information was incomplete. CEO John Stumpf left and the sales goals were dropped.

questions: Why pay reps per program signed?
Heartland fired 230 staff. Why didn't that fix it?
You are Walt's friend. What does loyalty to him require here?

press.headline: Heartland Beef Ends Sales Targets and Refunds Ranchers
press.story: The company dropped its five-programs bonus and will refund every disputed fee after an outside review. Ranchers called the apology overdue but welcome, while the lender raised the credit line rate and the plant cut two shifts as sales fell.

press.headline: Heartland Beef Adds Confirmation Calls, Keeps Sales Bonus
press.story: Reps will phone ranchers to confirm each sign-up, and anyone caught will be fired. The ranchers' co-op says firing more low-level staff misses the people who set the targets, and a state regulator asked for the complaint log.

press.headline: Heartland Beef Orders Six-Month Review of Sales Plan
press.story: The company says it takes the matter seriously but changes nothing now. The newspaper ran its story on schedule, and a state regulator has asked for the standard rancher contract.

press.headline: Heartland Beef Moves Top Sales Executive Out
press.story: Karen Mueller leaves the division, and an interim head will decide on targets after ninety days. Analysts noted the division brings in 60% of profit, and two regional managers resigned within the week.
